newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish President's aide Belka made finance chief.
newsitem.headline: Polish President's aide Belka made finance chief.

text.p: Grzegorz Kolodko quit on Tuesday after nearly three years as independent-minded finance minister in three Polish leftist coalition governments.
Presidential adviser Marek Belka took his place vowing continuity of policy.
Both Belka, 45, a non-party economics professor, and Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz stressed this did not herald a shift of direction. Financial markets reacted with calm.

"This personnel change does not signal the slightest changes in the government's economic policy, which so far has served Poland well," Cimoszewicz said at a hand-over ceremony at President Aleksander Kwasniewski's palace.
Kolodko said he wanted to return to academic life and avoid getting drawn into parliamentary elections due in September.
"Now we are entering an election campaign in which I do not want and will not take part," he said explaining his decision.

"The Polish economy is in Olympic shape and in the good hands of Professor Belka," Kolodko commented, saying he was leaving market reforms on course and had steered Poland into the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
The non-party Kolodko, 47, has often clashed with cabinet colleagues in the coalition linking Cimoszewicz's ex-communist SLD party and a smaller Peasant party.

There have been rumours of his departure since last year, when he furiously blamed taxpayers for taking advantage of a tax loophole left by his ministry, the authority of which was cut in a government reorganisation in October 1996.
Last month he criticised the cabinet after it gave in to Peasant party pressure and restored import duty on grain for animal feed, which Kolodko said threatened to boost inflation.

Opposition politicians speculated the decision to let him go now was aimed at dropping an unpopular minister in the build-up to the polls, in which a rightist alliance grouped around the Solidarity union is mounting a strong challenge.

"The election campaign is approaching and the SLD knows very well what it is doing. This is a classic pre-election move replacing an unpopular minister with a new man," said Jan Litynski, a senior member of the centrist Union for Freedom.
Cimoszewicz said he had no fundamental policy differences with Kolodko, but admitted they did not get on personally and that he had asked Kwasniewski to accept his resignation.

Kolodko has been widely seen as a defender of fiscal discipline and praised for continuing some market reforms launched after the 1989 fall of communism. He also drafted the coalition's medium and longer-term strategies.
During his time Poland had growth of five to seven percent of gross domestic product a year, although it failed to meet targets for cutting inflation, which was 18.5 percent in 1996.

But leading political or market analysts saw no threat that his replacement by Belka would harm the economy, and several praised the new minister's professional credentials while pointing out that he was so far untested in cabinet office.

"I know Professor Marek Belka as a very good economist... but I cannot say anything about his ability to make decisions in difficult matters such as economic policy," said liberal opposition leader Leszek Balcerowicz, who as finance minister from 1989 to 1991 launched Poland's market reforms.
Kolodko's old sparring partner, central bank president Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz, said experience showed Poland's prudent economic policy survived changes of finance ministers.
"Mr. Belka is certainly a proponent of anti-inflationary policy and of crucial and intensive structural changes in the economy," she said adding his work had lent him credibility.
Belka, who also took over Kolodko's title of deputy prime minister, told Reuters he would continue Kolodko's fight to curb inflation and reduce the budget deficit.
He said he wanted to speed up privatisation of banks and a reform of the inefficient social security system.

Belka, who has advised Kwasniewski on the economy since late 1995, promised to pursue the goals laid out in Kolodko's policy outlines, the Strategy for Poland and the Package 2000, which he said had been adopted by the entire government.
